extracted.intended_audience: travellers to Venice interested in art and architecture (tourists, students, connoisseurs)
extracted.subtask_description: A traveler's evaluative guide to what to see and how to judge paintings and buildings in Venice, with priorities for artists, advice on what details to notice, and how to avoid wasting time on second-rate works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate only on objects worth study
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate only the objects which are really worth his study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A traveller's interest is precious and limited: it is physically impossible to see and understand more than a certain quantity of art in a given time; attention bestowed on second-rate works is not merely lost but actually harmful — deadening interest and confusing the memory with respect to those which it is a duty to enjoy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise Tintoret, Paul Veronese, and John Bellini
rubrics_metrics.description: If fond of paintings, devote principal attention to the works of Tintoret, Paul Veronese, and John Bellini.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titian can be well studied in almost any great European gallery and is therefore less Venice-specific; Tintoret and Bellini can only be judged of in Venice, and Paul Veronese cannot be fully estimated until seen in Venetian ceilings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider conservation and legibility of works
rubrics_metrics.description: Give copious notices to works that are much injured, difficult to read, or neglected by other writers (notably Tintoret's works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because damage and neglect affect how works can be judged, injured or dirty pictures may require more commentary; restoration history and current condition must be taken into account when assessing merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-rely on assigned dates for buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: The dates assigned to various buildings are almost without exception conjectural (founded on internal evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some dates may be mistaken; occasional dating errors do not materially affect broader conclusions, but further inquiry may reveal specific misdatings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question admiration based on size or gaudiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how much of one's admiration depends merely upon a picture being larger than others and having bright masses of red and blue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size and gaudiness do not inherently make a picture better; the viewer should make the effort necessary to discover the merit of more profound and solemn works (e.g., Bellini, Tintoret) rather than being swayed by superficial attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paintings as sources of architectural and costume information
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine Carpaccio and Gentile Bellini carefully as they represent scenes in ancient Venice full of interesting architecture and costume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some pictures are valuable more for their documentary detail of architecture and costume than for painterly novelty; treat them as historical records as well as works of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer characteristic works over commonly quoted but unrepresentative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek characteristic examples of a master rather than accepting small or paltry works quoted as typical (e.g., avoid citing a paltry cenacolo as characteristic of Tintoret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of critics or handbooks that select unrepresentative works; good criticism distinguishes truly characteristic pieces from minor or atypical ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to architectural details to determine style and period
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe windows, orders, traceries, balconies, cornices, jambs, capitals, and mouldings to judge style, date, and influences (Gothic, Byzantine, Renaissance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many diagnostic features (sea story, entresol, Byzantine cornices, traceries) indicate period and influence; noting these details lets the traveler form accurate impressions of a building's character and date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess display and lighting conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer pictures that are in a fresh state and seen in a bright, not excessive, light so that parts of them are well seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good lighting and reasonable preservation allow reliable judgement; works hidden by poor lighting or obstructions (e.g., altar-temple concealing lower parts) cannot be properly assessed from close-up and may need viewing from intended vantage points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze composition and focal hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe what the painter has emphasized (who/what is principal or accessory) and how compositional choices guide the viewer's eye (e.g., Tintoret making principals accessory and accessories principal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study placement of major figures vs. foreground detail and the sequence in which attention is intended to be engaged (foreground, color patches, distant elements, then principal subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate colour usage and palette choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the presence or absence of bright tints, the painter's taste for certain hues (e.g., avoidance of light greens in vegetation), and the overall modesty or vividness of colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour should be read in terms of harmony, restraint, and specific technical choices (shadow greens, sober browns against crimson); these choices are integral to the artist's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge handling and manner of painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the painter's handling (noble manner, finish, heavy/overdone painting) and how these qualities affect the work's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work may be notable for 'handling' even if large or gaudy; conversely, over-finished or heavy painting often indicates failure of conception or later restoration/interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to over-labour and conventionalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify when a subject is hampered by types and conventionalities or over-labouring (e.g., Resurrection painted with Renaissance absurdities and over-finished cherubs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-laboured pictures may reveal the artist's discomfort with the subject or the imposition of patrons' expectations; these factors can detract from artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect restorations, reworkings, and scholar interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the possibility that parts of a picture have been redone by restorers or scholars rather than the master (e.g., figures that look like a scholar's work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uneven quality within a picture, dark/spoiled areas, or stylistic inconsistencies may indicate later repainting; such works may be 'not worth spending time on' if largely altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage time by prioritising truly worthy works in overwhelming collections
rubrics_metrics.description: In rooms with a multitude of works (e.g., Ducal Palace), refuse general attention and focus only on a short list of principal masterpieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large collections can weary the viewer; a recommended shortlist (e.g., Paradise by Tintoret, Siege of Zara, certain Titian and Tintoret works) helps concentrate study on the most important pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish historical from artistic interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that some works are valuable historically but not artistically (e.g., large battle pieces representing events rather than artistic invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such pictures as historically informative rather than as high artistic achievements; manage expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider intended viewing distance and vantage point
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works were executed for distant effect and are seen best from a particular spot or at the far end of a room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge monumental or ceiling paintings from too close; step back to their intended viewpoint to appreciate composition and effect (e.g., Christ taken down from the Cross seen best from the end of the room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe compositional organisation for complexity and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the structural organisation of very large compositions (e.g., concentric zones, belts of figures, central focal figures) as a measure of complexity and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting figures or noting the division into zones can help the observer understand the work's ambition and narrative architecture; such works may be 'read' in fragments by a patient observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of misattribution and low-quality imitators
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mistake the works of lesser or imitator artists (e.g., Domenico Robusti) for those of the master (Jacopo Tintoret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution errors are common; confirm authorship before attributing merit, especially in large collections where pupils or workshop assistants produced lesser works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate buildings in urban context and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge palaces and churches not just by isolated details but by their position, group effect, and views from particular angles (side views, relation to the Grand Canal, distant vistas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A building's overall effect (color, grouping with landmarks like the Rialto or La Salute, anchoring of shipping at the quay) contributes heavily to its value as an urban ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret proportion and 'fit' in context of function
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't criticise domestic Gothic buildings as 'ill-proportioned' without considering constraints of site and function; small houses may be beautiful and dignified despite diminutiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms should account for the building's functional needs (room size, balcony convenience) and the realities of the neighbouring urban fabric rather than abstract external proportions alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note the artist's characteristic motifs and grotesque tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe recurring motifs or eccentricities (e.g., love of grotesque sea-weeds, daring conception of green surges) as part of a master's signature style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognising these motifs helps identify an artist's hand and understand why certain works may feel wild, careless, or uniquely characteristic of the master.
